claims.text: Nearly equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi can form a single-phase FCC solid solution.
The proposed nanoparticles have diameters of 5–20 nm and contain approximately 20 at% each of Co, Cr, Fe, Mn, and Ni.
Inert-gas condensation or colloidal reduction can be used to synthesize the specified single-phase CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles.
Annealing between 0.3 Tm and 0.7 Tm for up to 100 hours followed by rapid quenching is the proposed thermal intervention.
Vacuum or argon prevents oxidation during annealing.
Nanoparticle structural stability is governed by competition between configurational-entropy stabilization and surface-energy-driven elemental segregation.
The component with the lowest surface energy segregates to the nanoparticle surface.
Surface segregation produces an enriched shell and a compositionally depleted core.
The nanoparticle surface-to-volume ratio creates a chemical-potential gradient that drives segregation.
The segregation-induced composition gradient lowers the activation energy for vacancy-mediated diffusion.
At moderate temperatures, the surface-segregation driving force overrides configurational-entropy stabilization in these nanoparticles.
Surface segregation and the resulting composition gradient enhance atomic mobility relative to bulk material.
High configurational entropy can stabilize bulk multicomponent solid solutions against phase separation or precipitation.
Bulk high-entropy alloys exhibit low or sluggish atomic diffusion because of severe lattice distortion.
After annealing, nanoparticle diffusion coefficients will be one to two orders of magnitude higher than values predicted by bulk HENA models.
Enhanced mobility may lead to intermetallic precipitation, phase separation, or amorphization not observed in corresponding bulk samples.
Surface effects become negligible for nanoparticles larger than 50 nm.
The segregation mechanism fails when component surface-energy differences are below 0.1 J/m².
Atomic diffusion is kinetically frozen below 0.2 Tm.
Homogeneous sub-20-nm particles with no surface segregation and diffusion coefficients no greater than bulk values after annealing would falsify the proposed surface-driven instability.
